case_name: McGill University c. Students for Palestine's Honour and Resistance McGill

McGill University c. Students
for Palestine's Honour and Resistance McGill

2025 QCCS 2964

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

montreal

No.:

500-17-133705-254

DATE:

August 4, 2025

_____________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

LOUIS CHARETTE, J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________

MCGILL UNIVERSITY

Plaintiff

v.

STUDENTS FOR PALESTINE’S
HONOUR AND RESISTANCE MCGILL

Defendant

and

STUDENTS’
SOCIETY OF MCGILL UNIVERSITY

Impleaded party

and

ASSOCIATION
OF MCGILL UNIVERSITY SUPPORT EMPLOYEES

ASSOCIATION OF MCGILL UNIVERSITY RESEARCH
EMPLOYEES

and

ASSOCIATION
OF GRADUATE STUDENTS EMPLOYED AT MCGILL

Intervenors

and

HILLEL
MONTREAL ET AL.

Intervening parties

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

(opposition to a voluntary conservatory
intervention)

_____________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

Commencing on April 2, 2025, a three-day student
strike on the campus of McGill University (“McGill”) led to violent clashes,
the blockading of buildings, the disruption and cancelling of classes, and acts
of vandalism and intimidation directed against the McGill’s administration,
students, professors and staff. On April 8, 2025, McGill filed an Originating
Application seeking provisional, interlocutory and permanent orders of
injunction against Students for Palestine’s Honour and Resistance McGill (“SPHR”)
to restore a climate of security on campus. It alleges that in the context of
the conflict in the Middle East following Hamas’ attack on Israel on October 7,
2023, SPHR has repeatedly participated and encouraged acts of violence on
McGill campus.

[
2
]

SPHR is an amorphous group of anonymous
individuals that calls for student action against McGill. It has not appeared
in the court record, nor has it been present or represented at any of the hearings
in the context of these proceedings.

[
3
]

In its Originating Application McGill names as
an impleaded party, Student’s Society of McGill University (“SSMU”) which
represents McGill undergraduate students.

[
4
]

A provisional injunction was granted for a
10-day period on April 15, 2025, essentially ordering the SPHR not to engage in
harassment, intimidation or the use of threats and not to impede access to
McGill buildings or otherwise interfere with academic activities.
[1]
The Application for a safeguard order was, however, subsequently
denied.
[2]
The Court of Appel dismissed the
application for authorization to appeal from this judgment.
[3]

[
5
]

Association of McGill University Support
Employees (“AMUSE”), Association
of McGill University Research Employees (“AMURE”) and Association of Graduate Students Employed at McGill (“AGSEM”), which represent various McGill employees filed declarations of voluntary aggressive interventions on April
24, 2025. Neither McGill nor SSMU opposed these interventions.

[
6
]

The hearing of the interlocutory injunction is
set on September 18 and 19, 2025.

[
7
]

On May 8, 2025, Hillel Montreal, Hillel McGill, McGill
Jewish Law Students Association, Chabad at McGill, Israel on Campus McGill, Students
Supporting Israel at McGill and Alpha Epsilon Pi McGill, who have identified
themselves as the “Jewish Student Associations” (“JSA”) filed a Declaration of
Voluntary Conservatory Intervention. They seek to intervene as parties in support
of McGill’s Application for the issuance of interlocutory and permanent
injunctions.

[
8
]

On May 20, 2025, SSMU filed an Opposition to the
reception of JSA’s Declaration of Voluntary Conservatory Intervention. AMUSE,
AMURE and AGSEM also contest
the intervention. For the purpose of the present judgment, the Court refers to these
four parties collectively as the “Opposing Parties”.

ANALYSIS

Legal principles

[
9
]

Article 184 C.C.P. allows a person who has
an interest in a proceeding but is not a party to voluntarily intervene in the
proceeding. The intervention is termed conservatory when the person wishes to
be joined with one of the parties to assist it or support its claims.
[4]

[
10
]

Where a party opposes the intervention,
[5]
the Court must determine whether the party seeking to intervene has
an interest as per article 85 C.C.P.

[
11
]

In the context of a purely private dispute, the
interest of a third person must be direct and personal.
[6]
However, where the litigation raises issues of public interest, the
person’s interest must be plausible. In
Boucher
c.
Pelletier
, the
Court of Appeal defines the plausible interest as follows:

[13] Il suffit donc au stade de la
réception que l’intervenant démontre un intérêt vraisemblable pour que l’intervention
soit reçue. Le mot « vraisemblable » signifie « qui paraît
vrai, qui a l’apparence de la vérité ». Les dictionnaires emploient le
mot « probable » pour décrire le mot « vraisemblable ».

[14] Le mot « vraisemblable »
veut dire « qui a une apparence de vérité ou le caractère de ce qui offre
toutes les probabilités ».
[7]

[
12
]

The Court of Appeal has also noted that the
approach in determining whether a third party possesses an interest must be
flexible and liberal.
[8]
Where the opposition to the third person’s
declaration of voluntary conservatory intervention is based on a lack on
interest, the party raising the opposition must demonstrate that the interest
is manifestly absent.
[9]

[
13
]

Moreover, the third party seeking to intervene must
demonstrate the useful purpose (“caractère opportune”) of its intervention in
that, it will bring additional insight as to the issues different from that of
the other parties.
[10]
As noted by the Court of Appeal, “[a]n intervention
should not be the mere repetition of similar positions in the hope of
amplifying their importance.”
[11]
The intervention should not, however, transform or otherwise expand
on the issues in litigation.
[12]

Discussion

[
14
]

The JSA’s Declaration of Voluntary Conservatory
Intervention sets out that they wish to intervene to support the conclusions
sought by McGill. Each has filed a sworn statement setting out its constitution
and mandate. The affiants further describe events which they have personally
been a victim of or have witnessed as a result of the strike, and of the
increased tension on campus.

[
15
]

The Opposing Parties raise four issues to oppose
the JSA’s Declaration of Voluntary Conservatory Intervention.

[
16
]

They first submit that the JSA do not possess
sufficient interest to intervene.

[
17
]

The argument must fail for three reasons. First,
it takes an overly narrow and restrictive approach to the determination of
interest. As noted by the Court of Appeal, where the litigation includes issues
of public interest, a flexible and liberal approach must be favoured to
determine whether a party has a plausible interest.

[
18
]

Although McGill’s Application may at first
glance appear as a private dispute, there can be no denying that issues of public
interest are at the heart of the litigation. These include rights protected by
the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
[13]
and the
Charter of Human Rights and
Freedoms
[14]
such as the freedom of religion, freedom of
thought, belief and opinion and every person’s right to liberty, security and
freedom of speech.

[
19
]

This conclusion is supported by the fact that
neither McGill nor SSMU opposed the interventions of AMUSE, AMURE and AGSEM. The latter have clearly indicated that they contest McGill’s Application
based on their right to freedom of speech in the context of their potential
labour disputes with McGill.

[
20
]

Furthermore, although none of the JSA are
physical persons, each is either an association or a non-profit corporation. Their
mandates may be summarized as follows: 1. defending the interests of Jewish
McGill students, including their right to openly express their opinions; and 2.
the expression of a positive image of the State of Israel and defending the
right of Jewish and non-Jewish students to openly discuss their affinity with
the State of Israel.

[
21
]

Although the Opposing Parties rightfully point
the fact that some of the JSA have no active members and that the decision to
intervene was taken only by the executive members and not the full membership, this
argument goes to the credibility and weight of their evidence not to their
interest.

[
22
]

In addition, the sworn statements refer to
specific events affecting the safety and security of Jewish students on McGill
campus. They raise concerns about the atmosphere of intimidation and hostility
towards Jewish students at McGill.

[
23
]

The judgment on the interlocutory and a
permanent injunction will inevitably have an impact on the JSA’s and their
members’ interests and rights. Although it may be true that none of the JSA
have alleged an immediate impact on an activity or event, the fact remains that
their members suffer the immediate consequences of the intimidation and
hostility towards Jewish students like none of the other parties currently
involved in the litigation.

[
24
]

The Court therefore concludes that the JSA have
demonstrated a plausible interest.

[
25
]

Second, the Opposing Parties argue that the JSA
seeks to modify and expand on the issues in litigation. The Court disagrees.

[
26
]

McGill’s Originating Application includes the
following allegation:

[71] On April 4, 2025, McGill sent
a notice to the SSMU terminating the memorandum of agreement between them,
exercising a contractual right that either party was permitted to exercise even
absent default, as appears from the letter communicated in support hereof as
Exhibit P-38. The notice referred to the SSMU’s deep lack of judgment in
encouraging this “strike” in an already tense campus climate, especially when
it lacked the ability to ensure that the strike would remain “peaceful” and
“voluntary” as was supposed intended.

[
27
]

JSA’s Declaration of Voluntary Conservatory
Intervention alleges as follows:

[3]  Since the events of October 7,
2023, the Defendant Students for Palestine’s Honour And Resistance McGill
(“SPHR”), the Mise-en-cause Students’ Society of McGill University (“SSMU”),
and their allies and supporters have either engaged in, promoted, encouraged or
tolerated conduct and tactics – including violence, physical assaults,
intimidation and property damage – which have created a toxic atmosphere for
Jewish students, including students of Israeli, on the McGill University campus
(the “Impugned Conduct”).

[
28
]

JSA’s allegation is in keeping with McGill’s and
does not change the nature of the issues nor does it add or complexify the
matter. This finding is supported by the fact that in the conclusions of their Declaration,
the JSA seek no relief other than what is sought by McGill.

[
29
]

The Opposing Parties raise a third argument with
respect to the intervention sought. They submit that in its Originating
Application, McGill refers to the impact of the strike and of other events on Jewish
and Israeli students
[15]
such that the JSA’s intervention merely
seeks to amplify the evidence in this regard and is therefore not necessary.

[
30
]

It cannot be denied that there is overlap
between McGill’s allegations and those of the JSA’s Declaration. However, such
is the very nature of a voluntary conservatory intervention.

[
31
]

The issue is rather whether the JSA’s
Declaration contributes to the Court’s ability to understand the issues in
litigation. In this regard, the JSA and their members can provide firsthand
insight on the intimidation, harassment and hostility towards Jewish students
and their allies. None of the other parties currently involved in the
litigation can do so with the same depth of knowledge.

[
32
]

Finally, the Opposing Parties submit that the
JSA’s Declaration of Intervention should be dismissed in the interest of the
guiding principle of proportionality.
[16]
This
argument must also fail.

[
33
]

McGill has clearly set out to restore a climate
of security on campus and in so doing, seeks to protect the interests of Jewish
students. It approaches the issue from its institutional perspective and its
obligations to staff and students.

[
34
]

SSMU is named as an impleaded party because of
its role in the three-day strike of April 2025 and because of its influence
over its members to communicate rules for protest and keeping the peace.
[17]
It contests the conclusions sought by McGill. AMUSE, AMURE and AGSEM also contest these conclusions. Neither
the Impleaded Party nor the Intervenors seek to represent the position of
McGill’s Jewish community despite the fact that their own membership may
include members of this community.

[
35
]

Hence, in determining whether allowing the JSA’s
Intervention is keeping with the principle of proportionality, the Court must
consider the fact that no other party to the litigation represents the Jewish
students who are directly affected by the current atmosphere on McGill campus. They
offer a unique perspective on the facts and the issues.

[
36
]

The Opposition to the JSA’s Declaration of
Voluntary Conservatory Intervention is therefore ill-founded and must be
dismissed.

FOR
THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
37
]

DISMISSES
Student’s
Society of McGill University’s Opposition to the Declaration of Voluntary
Conservatory Intervention dated May 8, 2025 filed by Hillel Montreal, Hillel
McGill, McGill Jewish Law Students Association, Chabad at McGill, Israel on
Campus McGill, Students Supporting Israel at McGill and Alpha Epsilon Pi McGill;

[
38
]

AUTHORIZES
the
Voluntary Conservatory Intervention of Hillel Montreal, Hillel McGill, McGill
Jewish Law Students Association, Chabad at McGill, Israel on Campus McGill, Students
Supporting Israel at McGill and Alpha Epsilon Pi McGill as per their
Declaration dated May 8, 2025;

[
39
]

Judicial costs to follow.
